sharpe.label: Sharpe ratio
sharpe.short: Return earned for each unit of risk taken.
sharpe.body: For every unit of price swing this investment put you through, it returned this many units of return above cash. It treats upside and downside swings as equally bad, which is why we show Sortino next to it.
sharpe.scale: Above 1.0 is generally considered good, above 2.0 excellent.
sharpe.caveat: Sharpe ratios estimated over a few years carry a lot of uncertainty — the range shown after the ± is the 95% confidence interval. If two investments' ranges overlap heavily, the difference between them is probably noise.

sortino.label: Sortino ratio
sortino.short: Return earned for each unit of downside risk taken.
sortino.body: Like Sharpe, but only counts downward swings as risk. Upside surprises don't count against it. Usually higher than Sharpe; a Sortino much higher than the Sharpe means most of this investment's volatility was to the upside.
sortino.scale: Above 1.0 is generally considered good, above 2.0 excellent.

calmar.label: Calmar ratio
calmar.short: Annual return per unit of worst drawdown.
calmar.body: How much annual return you got for the worst peak-to-trough fall you would have lived through. The most intuitive risk-adjusted ratio: return per unit of worst pain.
calmar.scale: Above 0.5 is decent, above 1.0 is strong.

martin.label: Martin ratio (UPI)
martin.short: Annual return per unit of the Ulcer Index.
martin.body: Like Calmar, but uses the whole drawdown path — how deep and how long — rather than just the single worst point. A more complete picture of how uncomfortable the ride was.
martin.scale: Higher is better; compare it only against other instruments over the same period.

volatility.label: Volatility
volatility.short: How much the price swings, annualised.
volatility.body: The annualised standard deviation of daily returns. Shown for reference, but deliberately not the headline risk figure here — research shows investors feel drawdowns, not day-to-day wiggle, so we lead with max drawdown instead.

maxDrawdown.label: Max drawdown
maxDrawdown.short: The worst peak-to-trough fall over this period.
maxDrawdown.body: If you had bought at the worst possible moment, this is how far down you would have been before it recovered — the single number that best predicts whether a real investor would have panic-sold.

timeUnderWater.label: Time under water
timeUnderWater.short: How long it took to get back to even.
timeUnderWater.body: The span from the prior peak to full recovery. This is the number that actually determines whether a retail investor capitulates — not the depth of the fall, but how long they'd have had to wait it out.

ulcerIndex.label: Ulcer Index
ulcerIndex.short: A single number for how deep and how long the drawdowns were.
ulcerIndex.body: Squares each day's drawdown depth before averaging, so it penalises deep, prolonged declines far more than brief dips — closer to how a loss actually feels than plain volatility.

var95.label: Value at Risk (95%)
var95.short: The threshold for a bad-but-not-worst day.
var95.body: On the worst 1 day in 20 over this period, the loss was at least this large. It says nothing about how much worse the remaining 5% of days could get — see CVaR for that.

cvar95.label: Expected shortfall (95%)
cvar95.short: The average loss on the worst days.
cvar95.body: The average loss across only the worst 5% of days — answers "and when it is that bad, how bad on average?". Strictly more informative than VaR alone.

beta.label: Beta
beta.short: How much this moves for each 1% move in the benchmark.
beta.body: A beta of 1.2 means it typically moved 1.2% when the benchmark moved 1%.
beta.caveat: Always check the R² next to it: if R² is low, the benchmark explains very little of this instrument's movement and the beta isn't telling you much.

alpha.label: Alpha (annualised)
alpha.short: Return left over after accounting for market exposure.
alpha.body: The annualised return this instrument produced beyond what its beta to the benchmark would predict.
alpha.caveat: A single-factor alpha against one benchmark is not strong evidence of skill — check its own confidence interval and R² before reading much into it.

rSquared.label: R²
rSquared.short: How much of the movement the benchmark actually explains.
rSquared.body: The share of this instrument's variance explained by the benchmark in the beta/alpha regression. Professionals always check this next to beta — a beta from a regression with low R² is mostly noise.

upCapture.label: Up capture
upCapture.short: How much of the benchmark's up days this captured.
upCapture.body: On days the benchmark rose, this instrument captured this percentage of that move on average.

downCapture.label: Down capture
downCapture.short: How much of the benchmark's down days this captured.
downCapture.body: On days the benchmark fell, this instrument captured this percentage of that fall on average. Lower is better here — it means smaller losses on the benchmark's bad days.

informationRatio.label: Information ratio
informationRatio.short: Active return per unit of tracking error versus the benchmark.
informationRatio.body: The right way to answer "was this better than the index, and how consistently?" — active return divided by how much that return varied.

trackingError.label: Tracking error
trackingError.short: How much this instrument's return diverges from the benchmark's.
trackingError.body: The annualised volatility of the return difference between this instrument and the benchmark. A near-index fund has a tracking error close to zero.

correlation.label: Correlation
correlation.short: How closely two instruments move together.
correlation.body: From −1 to +1. Above about 0.8 means holding both gives you much less diversification than it looks like — they will usually move together.
correlation.scale: Below 0.3 is meaningfully diversifying; above 0.8 is close to redundant.

downsideCorrelation.label: Downside correlation
downsideCorrelation.short: Correlation measured only on the benchmark's worst days.
downsideCorrelation.body: Diversification matters most exactly when things go wrong, and correlations usually rise in a crash.
downsideCorrelation.caveat: If this number is much higher than the headline correlation, these two won't protect you when it counts.

diversificationRatio.label: Diversification ratio
diversificationRatio.short: How much combining these actually reduced risk.
diversificationRatio.body: The weighted average of each instrument's own volatility, divided by the volatility of holding them together in equal weight. A ratio well above 1.0 means real diversification benefit; near 1.0 means holding them together barely helped.

cagr.label: CAGR
cagr.short: Compound annual growth rate over this period.
cagr.body: The constant annual growth rate that would take the starting price to the ending price over this exact span, on a calendar-day basis so periods of different lengths are comparable.

cumulativeReturn.label: Cumulative return
cumulativeReturn.short: Total return over the whole period, uncompounded to a yearly rate.
cumulativeReturn.body: How much a single investment made or lost from the start of the period to the end, including dividends.

trailingPe.label: Trailing P/E
trailingPe.short: Price divided by the last 12 months of earnings.
trailingPe.body: How many years of current earnings you're paying for at today's price. Always read against a peer or sector reference — a P/E of 28 means nothing on its own.
trailingPe.caveat: Undefined or misleading when earnings are negative or unusually depressed/inflated.

forwardPe.label: Forward P/E
forwardPe.short: Price divided by next year's expected earnings.
forwardPe.body: Like trailing P/E, but based on analyst estimates rather than reported results — more forward-looking, but only as reliable as the estimates behind it.
forwardPe.caveat: Depends on analyst consensus estimates, which can be wrong or sparse for smaller names.

priceToBook.label: Price to book
priceToBook.short: Price relative to accounting net asset value.
priceToBook.body: How the market values the company relative to what its balance sheet says it's worth.
priceToBook.caveat: Close to meaningless for asset-light software businesses; for financials it is often the primary valuation metric.

evToEbitda.label: EV / EBITDA
evToEbitda.short: Enterprise value relative to operating earnings.
evToEbitda.body: Capital-structure-neutral, so it compares companies fairly regardless of how much debt they carry — the multiple professionals actually use for cross-company comparison.

evToSales.label: EV / Sales
evToSales.body: The fallback valuation multiple when earnings are negative — which is exactly when P/E goes blank.

dividendYield.label: Dividend yield
dividendYield.short: Annual dividends as a percentage of price.
dividendYield.body: How much cash income the current price buys you per year, before any price change.
dividendYield.caveat: A high yield alone can be a warning sign (a "yield trap") — always check the payout ratio next to it to see whether the dividend is sustainable.

payoutRatio.label: Payout ratio
payoutRatio.short: The share of earnings paid out as dividends.
payoutRatio.body: What fraction of profit goes to dividends rather than being reinvested or retained. A ratio near or above 100% leaves little cushion if earnings dip.

fcfYield.label: Free cash flow yield
fcfYield.short: Free cash flow as a percentage of market value.
fcfYield.body: Free cash flow is harder to manipulate with accounting choices than reported earnings, and it's defined even when P/E is not (negative earnings).

roe.label: Return on equity
roe.short: Profit generated per unit of shareholder equity.
roe.body: A quality measure: how efficiently the company turns shareholders' capital into profit.
roe.caveat: Leverage inflates ROE mechanically — always check debt/equity alongside it.

debtToEquity.label: Debt / equity
debtToEquity.short: Total debt relative to shareholder equity.
debtToEquity.body: A core solvency measure — high leverage is the single best predictor of permanent capital loss in a downturn.

expenseRatio.label: Expense ratio
expenseRatio.short: The fund's annual fee, taken automatically from its value.
expenseRatio.body: The most reliable predictor of how a fund performs against its peers — in any market, net returns equal gross returns minus costs, so the low-cost fund tends to win by arithmetic.
expenseRatio.caveat: A 1%/year difference compounds to roughly a quarter of terminal wealth over 30 years.

psr.label: Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio
psr.short: The probability the true Sharpe ratio is genuinely above zero.
psr.body: Converts a point estimate into a confidence statement, accounting for sample size, skew and fat tails — the honest version of "is this actually good, or did it just get lucky?"
psr.caveat: A statement about the past, calculated from the sample shown — not a forecast.

honesty.title: Read this before you trust the numbers above

hindsight.title: Hindsight
hindsight.body: You chose these dates knowing what happened. This shows what did happen in this window, not what will happen next.

survivorship.title: Survivorship bias
survivorship.body: You can only backtest instruments that still exist and are still listed. Companies that went to zero are not in this dataset. Research on the US market (Bessembinder, 2018) found the median listed stock underperformed Treasury bills over its lifetime — the winners you can still see are the survivors.

deflated.title: Adjusted for how many tries this took
deflated.body: You have run {{nTrials}} backtests. Even with no skill at all, the best of that many tries would be expected to show a Sharpe of about {{expected}} by luck alone. This one's is {{actual}}.

twr.label: Time-weighted return
twr.short: How the investment performed, ignoring when you added money.
twr.body: Time-weighted return measures how the investment performed, ignoring when you added money. It is what a fund reports.

mwr.label: Money-weighted return
mwr.short: How you performed, including the timing of your contributions.
mwr.body: Money-weighted return (IRR) measures how you performed, including the timing of your contributions. If it is lower than the time-weighted return, your money arrived at less fortunate moments — which is normal and mostly luck.

deflatedSharpe.label: Deflated Sharpe ratio
deflatedSharpe.short: Sharpe, adjusted for how many scenarios you have tried.
deflatedSharpe.body: When you try many strategies, the best-looking one is partly lucky. This adjusts the score for how many scenarios you have run, so a good-looking result has to be genuinely good rather than the best of many tries.

entrySensitivity.label: Entry-date sensitivity
entrySensitivity.short: How much the result depends on the exact day you started.
entrySensitivity.body: The same investment started a few weeks earlier or later. A wide spread means the result depends heavily on the exact day you picked — which you chose knowing what happened next.

costDrag.label: Cost drag
costDrag.body: Trading fees, compounded. Small percentages become large amounts over long periods — this is the single most reliable way to improve returns, because unlike returns, costs are certain.

price.title: Price

levels.title: Key price levels
levels.empty: Not enough confirmed pivots yet to identify a level.
levels.caption: Price areas where this instrument has repeatedly reversed. They are not floors or ceilings — they break regularly.

panes.rsiOverboughtMuted: Overbought/oversold lines are muted — less meaningful in a strong trend.
panes.obvDivergenceHint: Shaded range: price and volume flow have been moving in different directions.

signals.title: What the indicators are saying together
signals.footer: Professional analysts look for agreement across several indicators. Disagreement is information too — it usually means no clear signal.

priceVsSma200.above: Price is above its 200-day moving average, a conventional (if crude) long-term uptrend marker.
priceVsSma200.below: Price is below its 200-day moving average, a conventional (if crude) long-term downtrend marker.
priceVsSma200.neutral: Price is within 1% of its 200-day moving average — too close to call a clear trend from this alone.

smaCross.golden: The 50-day average is above the 200-day average (a “golden cross” regime) — a conventional bullish trend marker.
smaCross.death: The 50-day average is below the 200-day average (a “death cross” regime) — a conventional bearish trend marker.
smaCross.neutral: The 50- and 200-day averages are too close to call a clear regime.

rsi.trending_overbought: RSI is {{rsi}}, above the conventional 70 “overbought” line. But ADX is {{adx}}, which says this instrument is in a strong trend — and in strong trends RSI routinely stays above 70 for weeks or months. In this context an elevated RSI is much weaker evidence than it would be in a sideways market.
rsi.ranging_overbought: RSI is {{rsi}} and ADX is {{adx}}, meaning price has been moving sideways rather than trending. Overbought readings have historically been more meaningful in range-bound conditions than in trending ones — but ‘more meaningful’ is not the same as reliable.
rsi.trending_oversold: RSI is {{rsi}}, below the conventional 30 “oversold” line, while ADX ({{adx}}) shows a strong trend in place — in a strong downtrend RSI can stay depressed for a long time.
rsi.ranging_oversold: RSI is {{rsi}} and ADX is {{adx}} (range-bound). Oversold readings have historically carried a little more weight in sideways conditions.
rsi.random_walk: Statistically, this instrument's recent price movements are indistinguishable from a random walk (variance-ratio test, p={{p}}). Trend-following indicators assume the opposite. Treat what follows as description, not prediction.
rsi.neutral: RSI is {{rsi}}, within the conventional 30–70 neutral band.

macd.bullish: The MACD histogram is positive and rising — short-term momentum has turned upward relative to the longer term. This is a lagging measure by construction.
macd.bearish: The MACD histogram is negative and falling — short-term momentum has turned downward relative to the longer term. This is a lagging measure by construction.
macd.neutral: The MACD histogram is close to zero — no clear momentum shift either way right now.

bollinger.above: Price is above the upper Bollinger Band (%B > 1). Price spends about 95% of its time inside the bands, so this is uncommon but not exceptional on its own.
bollinger.below: Price is below the lower Bollinger Band (%B < 0).
bollinger.inside: Price is within the Bollinger Bands (0 ≤ %B ≤ 1), where it spends most of its time.

obv.divergence_bearish: Price has been making new highs while on-balance volume has not — the move looks like it is happening on thinner participation than the last one.
obv.divergence_bullish: Price has been making new lows while on-balance volume has not fallen with it — selling pressure looks like it may be thinning.
obv.confirming: On-balance volume is moving in the same direction as price, with no divergence detected over the trailing window.
obv.unavailable: Volume data isn't available for this instrument, so OBV can't be computed.

adx.context: ADX measures trend strength, not direction. At {{adx}} this instrument is {{state}} — use it to weigh how much to trust the trend-following indicators above.

signals.lowConfidenceNote: Lower confidence: short history, an insignificant random-walk test, or thin volume weakens this reading.

monteCarlo.title: Possible paths from here

modelHints.bootstrap: Resamples blocks of this instrument's own historical daily moves, which preserves real patterns of calm and turbulent stretches.
modelHints.gbm: The textbook random-walk model: returns drawn from a normal distribution. Its tails are visibly thinner than what markets actually produce.
modelHints.student_t: A normal-shaped model with fatter tails than the plain bell curve, closer to how markets actually behave but still not a resampling of real history.

monteCarlo.sentenceIntro: Based on how {{symbol}} has actually behaved over the past {{years}} years, in {{horizon}} trading days:
monteCarlo.bulletMiddleHalf: the middle half of simulated outcomes land between {{low}} and {{high}}
monteCarlo.bulletAboveToday: {{pct}} of paths finish above today's price
monteCarlo.bulletDrawdown20: in {{pct}} of paths, the price fell more than 20% at some point along the way
monteCarlo.calibrationNote: This is not a forecast. It resamples {{symbol}}'s actual daily moves from {{start}} to {{end}} in blocks, which preserves its real pattern of calm and turbulent stretches. It assumes {{driftNote}}. It cannot know about anything that has not happened before — an earnings surprise, a takeover, a market crash of a new kind.
monteCarlo.calibrationVolNote: Current volatility is in the {{percentile}}th percentile of the last three years, so if conditions return to normal, the real range would be wider than shown.
monteCarlo.driftNoteZero: no expected drift, so it says nothing about direction
monteCarlo.driftNoteHistorical: a historical drift of {{drift}}/yr (±{{se}} standard error — treat the direction with real skepticism)
monteCarlo.driftNoteRiskFree: drift at the risk-free rate, the risk-neutral convention

rsi.label: RSI
rsi.body: A 0–100 momentum gauge comparing recent gains to recent losses. Above 70 is conventionally called 'overbought', below 30 'oversold'. These are conventions, not laws — in a strong trend RSI can sit above 70 for months while the price keeps rising. Read it alongside the trend strength shown above.

macd.label: MACD
macd.body: The gap between a fast and a slow moving average. When the bars flip from below to above zero, short-term momentum has turned upward relative to the longer term. It is a lagging measure by construction — it describes what has already changed.

bollinger.label: Bollinger Bands
bollinger.body: A moving average with bands two standard deviations above and below. Price spends about 95% of its time inside the bands, so touching a band is common, not exceptional. When the bands squeeze tight, the instrument has been unusually calm — and calm periods have historically been more often followed by large moves, in either direction.

atr.label: ATR
atr.body: The typical size of a day's price range, in currency. An ATR of 4.20 means a 4 move on a given day is ordinary, not news. Traders use it to size stop-losses; long-term investors can use it to calibrate what 'normal' looks like.

obv.label: OBV
obv.body: Adds the day's volume when price closes up and subtracts it when price closes down. If price is making new highs while this line is not, the move is happening on thinner trading than the previous one.

adx.label: ADX
adx.body: Measures how strongly price is trending, without saying in which direction. Below 20 means sideways; above 25 means a real trend is in place. It is the context that decides how much weight to give the other indicators.

varianceRatio.label: Variance ratio test
varianceRatio.body: A statistical test of whether price movements have any memory. If the result is not significant, this instrument's recent movements are indistinguishable from coin flips — which is what most academic finance predicts, and it means trend indicators have little to work with here.

monteCarlo.label: Monte Carlo simulation
monteCarlo.body: Thousands of simulated futures built by reshuffling this instrument's own historical daily moves. It shows the range of what its past behaviour makes plausible — not a prediction. The width of the fan is the message.

supportResistance.label: Support & resistance
supportResistance.body: Price areas where this instrument has repeatedly stopped and turned around. They matter because other market participants watch them and place orders around them, which can make them partly self-fulfilling. They are not floors or ceilings — they break regularly.

states.insufficientHistory: Needs at least 200 days of history — this instrument has {{bars}}.
states.noVolume: Volume data isn't available for this instrument, so on-balance volume isn't shown.
states.crypto: Crypto trades 24/7, so daily-bar indicators here behave a little differently than for stocks.

footer.priceBasis: The price chart, moving averages and levels use unadjusted prices — the prices that actually traded — while volatility and the simulation use dividend-adjusted total-return prices.
